### a. Definitions {.unnumbered}

#### Classic causal inference








::: {#def-statistical-model .theorem}
## Statistical model

A statistical model is a collection of probability distributions on a set of random variables.

$$
\mathcal{M}=\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}\quad\text{on set of random variables }\mathbf V.
$$
:::

::: {#def-npsem-ie .theorem}
## NPSEM-IE

A nonparametric structural equation model with independent errors (NPSEM-IE) is a [statistical model](#def-statistical-model) in which each random variable is as deterministic function (defined by a structural equation) of other variables along with an error term. Error terms are mutually independent and no variable is direclty or indirectly a function of itself. 

$$
\mathscr M=\{f_{j}:V_j\in\mathbf V\}
$$
where 

$$
V_{j} \;=\; f_{j}\!\big( V_{1},\dots,V_{j-1},\, U_{j} \big),
$$

$$
\{U_j\}_{V_j \in \mathbf V} \ \text{ mutually independent.}
$$
:::

::: {#def-parent-child .theorem}
## Parent

In an [NPSEM-IE](#def-npsem-ie), if variable $X$ appears in the structural equation for $Y$, then $X$ is a parent of $Y$ and $Y$. The set of parents for $X$ is denoted $\mathbf{Pa}(X)$.

:::


::: {#def-observational-unit .theorem}
## Observational unit

An observational unit is a subset of the random variables in a [statistical model](#def-statistical-model) that originate from the same data source. The collection of observational units forms a partition of the full set of random variables. 

Given a set of variables $\mathbf V_i$ an observational unit is a set $\mathbf V$ such that:

$$
\mathbf V=\bigcup_{i=1}^n \mathbf V_i,\qquad \mathbf V_i\cap \mathbf V_j=\varnothing\ (i\ne j).
$$
:::

::: {#def-equivalence .theorem}
## Equivalence

Two random variables are equivalent if they belong to different [observational units](#def-observational-unit) but represent the same construct. 

$$
X_i\sim X_j\iff i\ne j;\ X_i\in \mathbf V_i;\ X_j\in \mathbf V_j,\ X_i, X_j \text{ represent same construct}.
$$
Two sets of random variables are equivalent if each element in one set has an equivalent in the other set.


:::










::: {#def-no-spillover .theorem}
## No spillover assumption

In an [NPSEM-IE](#def-npsem-ie), the *no spillover* assumption requires that no variable is a [parent](#def-parent-child) of an [equivalent](#def-equivalence) variable in another [observational unit](#def-observational-unit).

$$
X\notin \mathbf{Pa}(X')\quad
\forall\, X\sim X',\ X\in \mathbf V_i,\ X'\in \mathbf V_j,\ i\ne j.
$$
:::

::: {#def-no-interference .theorem}
## No interference assumption

In an [NPSEM-IE](#def-npsem-ie), the *no interference* assumption requires that no variable is a [parent](#def-parent-child) of any non-[equivalent](#def-equivalence) variable in another [observational unit](#def-observational-unit).

$$
X\notin \mathbf{Pa}(Y)\quad
\forall\, X\in \mathbf V_i,\ Y\in \mathbf V_j,\ i\ne j,\ X\not\sim Y.
$$
:::

::: {#def-identical-distributions .theorem}
## Identical distributions assumption

In an [NPSEM-IE](#def-npsem-ie), the *identical distributions* assumption requires that [equivalent](#def-equivalence) variables have identical structural equations.

$$
X_i\sim X_j\Rightarrow f_{X_i}=f_{X_j}.
$$
:::

::: {#def-intervention-ffrcistg .theorem}
## Intervention


An intervention is an ordered pair $(\mathscr{M}, \Gamma)$ which contains a NPSEM-IE $\mathscr{M}$, and a set of deterministic functions  
$$
\Gamma = \{ h_V  : V \in \mathbf V \text{ such that } h_V, f_V \text{ have identical arguments}\}
$$  

which are each indexed by one of the random variables in the model and have the same arguments as the structural equation $f_V \in \mathscr{M}$ for that variable.
:::

::: {#def-intervention-set .theorem}
## Intervention set

Given intervention $(\mathscr{M}, \Gamma)$, the intervention set is the subset of random variables associated with a function in $\Gamma$.


$$
\mathbf V^I = \{V : h_V \in \Gamma\} \subset  \mathbf V
$$






:::


::: {#def-counterfactual-npsem .theorem}
# Counterfactual NPSEM-IE

Given intervention $(\mathscr{M}, \Gamma)$, the counterfactual NPSEM-IE is defined


$$
\mathscr{M}^{(\Gamma)} =  \{f_V^{(\Gamma)}: V \in \mathbf V \}
$$

Where 

$$
f_V^{(\Gamma)} = \begin{cases}
  h_V & \text{if}  & V \in \mathbf V^I\\
  f_V & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$


:::

::: {#def-counterfactual-random-variables .theorem}
# Counterfactual random variable

Given intervention $(\mathscr{M}, \Gamma)$, with  $\mathscr{M} = \{f_V: V \in \mathbf V\}$ such that 

$$
V  \;=\; f_V\big( \mathbf{Pa}(V), U_V \big), \quad \{U_V\}_{V \in \mathbf V} \ \text{ mutually independent.}
$$

the counterfactual random variables are defined:

$$
V^{(\Gamma)}  \;=\; f_V^{(\Gamma)}\big( \mathbf{Pa}(V)^{(\Gamma)}, U_V \big)
$$


where 

$$ 
\mathbf{Pa}(V)^{(\Gamma)} = \{ W^{(\Gamma)}: W \in \mathbf{Pa}(V)\}
$$ 

Note that the $U_V$ represented as an argument for $f_V^{(\Gamma)}$ is identical in value to the $U_V$ represented as an argument for $f_V$. This is the basis of the "consistency" assumption.

:::

::: {#def-causal-model .theorem}
## Causal model

A causal model $\mathscr{C}$ is a statistical model of the observed and counterfactual random variables associated with a given set of interventions $\{(\mathscr{M},\Gamma_k)\}_{k\in \mathbf E }$. In this model, the error term for each counterfactual random variable is set as equal to the error term in the corresponding observed variable. 



$$
\mathscr{C} = \mathscr{M} \cup \{\mathscr{M}^{(\Gamma)}\}_{\Gamma \in \mathbf E} 
$$
With observed random variables associated with this model being

$$
V  \;=\; f_V\big( \mathbf{Pa}(V), U_V \big) \quad \{U_V\}_{V \in \mathbf V} \ \text{ mutually independent.}
$$


and counterfactual random variables


$$
V^{(\Gamma)}  \;=\; f_V^{(\Gamma)}\big( \mathbf{Pa}(V)^{(\Gamma)}, U_V \big)
$$

:::

::: {#def-ffrcistg .theorem}
## FFRCISTG model

A finest fully randomized causally interpretable structured tree graph (FFRCISTG) model is a causal model that satisfies the (1) [no spillover](#def-no-spillover), (2) [no interference](#def-no-interference), and (3) [identical distributions](#def-identical-distributions) assumptions. 


:::

#### Network causal inference


::: {#def-graph .theorem}
## Graph

A *[graph](#def-graph)* is an ordered pair $\mathscr{G} = (\mathcal{N}, \psi)$ with nodeset $\mathcal{N}$and adjacency function $\psi$ which assigns a nonnegative weight to each unordered pair of nodes $(i,j)$. 

$$
\mathscr G=(\mathcal N,\psi),\qquad
\psi:\mathcal N\times\mathcal N\to \mathbb R_{\ge 0},\qquad
\psi(i,j)=\psi(j,i)
$$

Nodes $i,j \in \mathcal{N}$ are connected if and only if $\psi(i,j) > 0$.
:::


::: {#def-neighborhood .theorem}
## Neighborhood

Given a [graph](#def-graph) $\mathscr{G} = (\mathcal{N}, \psi)$, the *[neighborhood](#def-neighborhood)* of a node $i \in \mathcal{N}$ is

$$
\mathcal{N}_i = \{ j \in \mathcal{N} : \psi(i,j) > 0 \}.
$$
:::

::: {#def-network-weights-vector .theorem}
## Network weights 

Given a [graph](#def-graph) $\mathscr{G} = (\mathcal{N}, \psi)$, the *[network weights vector](#def-network-weights-vector)* for a node $i \in \mathcal{N}$ is

$$
\Psi_i = [\psi(i,1), \dots, \psi(i,n)]^T,
\qquad n=|\mathcal N|.
$$
:::

::: {#def-network-values .theorem}
## Network values 

Given a [graph](#def-graph) $\mathscr{G} = (\mathcal{N}, \psi)$ with [neighborhood](#def-neighborhood) $\mathcal N_i$ for each node $i$, and given a vector $\mathbf X \in \{0,1\}^n$ indexed by nodes in $\mathscr{N}$, the *network values* for $i$ with respect to  $\mathbf X$ is the subvector of $\mathbf X$ indexed by $\mathscr{N}_i$.

$$
\mathbf X_{\mathcal N_i}=\big(X_j\big)_{j\in \mathcal N_i}.
$$
:::

::: {#def-exposure-mapping .theorem}
## Exposure mapping

Given an [NPSEM-IE](#def-npsem-ie) with $f_{Y_i}$ the [structural equation](#def-npsem-ie) for $Y_i$, and $\mathbf{X}_1,\dots,\mathbf{X}_K \in \{0,1\}^n$ the [parents](#def-parent-child) of $Y_i$, the exposure mapping for $f_{Y_i}$* is a function

$$
g_i : \{0,1\}^{K \times n} \to \mathbb{R}^m
$$

such that

$$
Y_i = f_{Y_i}\big(g_i(\mathbf{X}_1,\dots,\mathbf{X}_K), U_{Y_i}\big).
$$
:::

::: {#def-separability .theorem}
## Separability

An [exposure mapping](#def-exposure-mapping) $g_i$ is *[separable](#def-separability)* if it can be written:

$$
g_i(\mathbf{X}_1,\dots,\mathbf{X}_K) 
  = \big[ \begin{pmatrix} X_{1i} \\ \dots \\ X_{Ki} \end{pmatrix},\, g_{1i}(\mathbf{X}_1),\, \dots,\, g_{Ki}(\mathbf{X}_K)\big]^T,
$$

where each $g_{ti} : \{0,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is a *component function* of $g_i$. 

A structural equation is said to be separable if its exposure mapping is separable. 
:::



::: {#def-positional-invariance .theorem}
## Positional invariance
Let $\mathcal{N}_{ti}$ denote the [neighborhood](#def-neighborhood) of node $i$ in [graph](#def-graph) $\mathscr{G}_t = (\mathcal{N}, \psi_t)$. A [component function](#def-separability) $g_{ti}$ is *[positionally invariant](#def-positional-invariance)* with respect to $\mathscr{G}_t$ if for all $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{X}' \in \{0,1\}^n$


$$
\mathbf{X}_{\mathcal{N}_i} = \mathbf{M}\mathbf{X}'_{\mathcal{N}_j}, 
\quad 
\Psi_{i,\mathcal{N}_i} = \mathbf{M}\Psi_{j,\mathcal{N}_j}
\Rightarrow
g_{ti}(\mathbf{X}) = g_{tj}(\mathbf{X}').
$$

An exposure mapping shows positional invariance with respect to  $\{\mathscr{G}_t\}_{t \in [1:K]}$ if it is separable and all its component functions show positional invariance with respect to an element of  $\{\mathscr{G}_t\}_{t \in [1:K]}$. A structural equation is positionally invariant if its exposure mapping is positionally invariant. 
:::

::: {#def-boundedness .theorem}
## Boundedness

A [component function](#def-separability) $g_{ti}$ is *[bounded](#def-boundedness)* if there exists a finite set $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathbb{R}$ and a constant $c \in \mathbb{R}$, independent of the size of the network $|\mathcal{N}|$, such that for $\mathbf{X} \in \{0,1\}^n$

$$
g_{ti}(\mathbf{X}) \in \mathcal{D} \quad \text{ for }|\mathcal{D}|< c \in \mathbb{Z}.
$$

An exposure mapping is bounded if it is [separable](#def-separability) and all its component functions are bounded. 
:::

::: {#def-network-exposure-mapping .theorem}
## Network exposure mapping

A network exposure mapping with respect to [graph](#def-graph) $\mathscr{G}_t$  is defined as a [component function](#def-separability) which is [bounded](#def-boundedness) and [positionally invariant](#def-positional-invariance) with respect to  $\mathscr{G}_t$. 

:::

::: {#def-homogeneous-network-interference .theorem}
## Homogeneous network interference

An exposure mapping exhibits homogeneous network interference with respect to a [graph set](#def-graph) $\{\mathscr{G}_t\}_{t \in [1:K]}$ if it is separable and all its [component functions](#def-separability) are [network exposure mappings](#def-network-exposure-mapping).

:::



::: {#def-network-ffrcistg .theorem}
##  NFFRCISTG model

A network finest fully randomized causally interpretable structured tree graph (NFFRCISTG) model defined on $\{\mathscr{G}_t\}_{t \in [1:K]}$ is a causal model which satisfies the (1) [no spillover](#def-no-spillover), (2) [homogenous network interference](#def-no-interference) with respect to $\{\mathscr{G}_t\}_{t \in [1:K]}$, and (3) [identical distributions](#def-identical-distributions) assumptions. 


:::

#### Social and spatial inference

::: {#def-random-nodes-bipartite-graph .theorem}
## Random graph generator

A structural equation that produces the adjacency function (matrix) of a bipartite graph with conformable dimensions.

$$
f_\psi:\mathcal U\to \mathbb R_{\ge 0}^{|V_1|\times |V_2|},
\qquad
\psi = f_\psi(U_\psi),\quad \operatorname{supp}(\psi)\subseteq V_1\times V_2 \cup V_2\times V_1.
$$
:::

::: {#def-social-spatial-npsem .theorem}
## Random graph NPSEM-IE

An NPSEM-IE whose structural equations include random graph generators whose component functions are loyal to one or more random graphs included in the model.

$$
\mathscr M=\{f_V:V\in\mathbf V\}\cup\{f_\psi\},\qquad
\text{each }g_{ti}\text{ in exposure mappings is loyal to the generated graphs.}
$$
:::

::: {#def-homogeneous-network-interference .theorem}
## Homogeneous random network interference

In a random graph NPSEM-IE, an exposure mapping exhibits homogeneous random network interference if it is separable and bounded and each of its component functions is loyal to a random graph included in the model.

:::

::: {#def-social-spatial-ffrcistg .theorem}
## RNFFRCISTG

A RNFFRCISTG is a causal model where (1) the interventions in the model were conducted on a random graph NPSEM-IE. The model satisfies the (i) no spillover (exempting graph generators), (ii) homogeneous random network interference with respect to the random networks, and (iii) identical distributions assumptions.


:::




::: {#def-social-spatial-ffrcistg .theorem}
## BRNFFRCISTG model

A BRNFFRCISTG is a causal model where (1) the interventions in the model were conducted on a random graph NPSEM-IE. The model satisfies the (i) no spillover (exempting graph generators), (ii) homogeneous random network interference with respect to the random networks, and (iii) identical distributions assumptions.


:::
